segments.text: - Hello, everyone.
Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today, we're gonna be
talking about something

that I often see in the
one-minute design reviews
that we do here on the channel,

and that is how to enforce
consistent parameterization
across all the parts in your schematics.
Now, if you're like me,

you are using the parameters
in your schematics
when you generate a bill of materials.
It's a common practice,
and what that means

is you have to enforce
consistent parameterization
across all of your parts.

Now, there is a simple way
to do that inside of Altium,

and I'm gonna show you
how to do that today.
We'll take a look at a couple

of example one-minute
design review submissions
that we filmed in the past,
and then we'll show you
how to enforce consistent parameterization
using those projects.
Let's hop in and get started.
(bright upbeat music)

Now, if you've watched the
channel for any length of time,

and you've watched any of the
one-minute design reviews,
you will inevitably hear me say something
about parameterization in schematics.

And what do I mean when I
refer to parameterization?
Well, it's pretty simple.

When you look at a component
in a schematic sheet
or in your library,
there are a bunch of parameters,
and you can see those parameters
in the Properties panel inside of Altium.

Those parameters can
have any name you want,

and they can contain any
information you want.
And most of the time,
those parameters just contain
some basic technical information.

Things like voltage
limits, current values,
resistance values, simple stuff like that.

But one thing that's really
important for parameterizing
is the part number

for the part that you're
going to put into the design.
Because of course,
if you put an integrated circuit
or even a resistor or a capacitor,
we want to know the specific part
that you want to use in your design.
Now, if you maintain your own libraries,
you would put a parameter
for the manufacturer part number
into the part in the library,
but of course,

you could have parts
from third-party sources.
Those third-party sources

could have any number
of parameters in them,
and then you could also put a parameter

for the manufacturer part number
in those third-party parts

and put them directly
into your schematics.

No matter how you do it or
where the parts come from,
we want to make sure
that the specific manufacturer part number

is put into one of those
parameters for that part.
Unfortunately, in quite a few

of the design review
submissions that we receive,

we tend to see pretty
inconsistent parameterization.
Let's take a look at some examples.
Very nicely organized and parameterized,

but you forgot some of the
most important parameters.

The manufacturer part number
and the manufacturer name.
Your parameterization
for your components is all over the place.
Get it together, bro.

The first thing I notice
on some of the parameters
is that they're really inconsistent.
I noticed that a lot of your components
don't have any supply chain information
in the component parameters.

So clearly, we get varying
levels of parameterization

and varying levels of
consistency of parameterization.
At the end of the day,
there's really only two parameters

that you should care about
above all the others,

the manufacturer name and
the manufacturer part number.
Those two things are what are used
to identify the specific component
that you want to put into your design,
and you would use that information
to actually order the components
when you go to get the board assembled.

Same thing goes if you're
consigning assembly
to an assembly company.

They're going to want to know
the manufacturer part number

for every single part that
appears in that design,

and you want to put that
into the bill of materials.
When you have consistent parameter naming

and all of the parts include
a manufacturer part number,
that's gonna make it a lot easier
to export a bill of material
where all of the lines are filled in

with all of the required
information that's needed
to actually purchase the components
and put them into your PCB assembly.
Now, there is a way inside Altium
to very quickly see all of the parameters

that are attached to
our parts in our design.
Here, I have a design open,

and what we wanna do is access
the Parameter Manager tool
to be able to see all of those parameters.
Now, while I have this design open
inside the schematic editor,
what I need to do is go to the Tools menu,

and then select the
Parameter Manager option.
Now, in any given design,
there are a ton of different parameters
attached to different objects,

and this set of check boxes
at the top of this dialogue
allows me to control

which of the parameters I
want to view in the design.
Here, we're talking about the parts

that actually end up in
your bill of materials,
so I only want to select the parts option
in this checkbox right here.
The next thing I normally do
is exclude the system parameters,

and I don't normally use system
parameters anyways in parts,
but if you do,

you can exclude them by
just checking this box.
Once we click OK,
you'll see the Parameter Manager table
or Parameter Editor table opens,

and you'll be able to see all
of the different parameters

that appear on all the
parts in your design.
So here along the top,
you can see that we have
all these different parameters listed.

You'll see that a lot of
these boxes are empty,
and that's because those parameters

are only actually
attached to certain parts,

as you can see in this
section of the table.

Now, if we scroll over to the
right and we look at the top,
we can start to see

where the inconsistent
parameterization starts to arise
as we're looking at a given design.
For example, on these parts,

we have Manufacturer and
Manufacturer Part Number

as parameters right here
in this part of the table.

So, you can see that
these diodes from Vishay
have the parameters assigned to them,
but none of the other parts
have those parameters assigned to them.
And then over here,

you can see that we have a
column that says PartNumber.

That is generally referring to
the manufacturer part number.

Two parts have this parameter
with the part number assigned,
but none of the other parts do.
Now, this is exactly what I'm referring to

when I talk about
inconsistent parameterization.

Some of the parts have
these parameters assigned.

A lot of the parts in
this particular design

don't have any part
number assigned anywhere,
and even if they are assigned,
they're all under different names.
That makes it extremely difficult

to export a bill of
materials in a timely manner.

If you were to go and
export a bill of materials
from this design,
most of the information

that would be needed in
that bill of materials
will actually be blank.
If you were to take the bill of materials
exported from this design
and send it over to an assembler,

they're going to send
the bill of materials
right back to you,
and they're going to ask you to fill it in
with all the required information.
Next, let's take a look
at this other design from (indistinct),

and this design has much
better parameterization.

If we just open up the
Parameter Manager dialog
and we scroll over to the right,

we'll be able to see
that most of the parts

actually have a manufacturer
name and part number filled in.

The manufacturer name
appears in this column,
and as I scroll down,

you see very few blank
entries in this design.

You can also see here that
there's a column for Mfr PN,
or manufacturer part number.

And again, you can see
that if we scroll down,
most of the parts in this design

are all filled in with a
manufacturer part number.

Now you might be wondering,
what's all of this blank space

that we have right here
starting in this row?
Well, if we scroll to the left,

we can see here that most
of those are test points.

In fact, all of those blank
entries are for test points.

And of course, those don't
have a manufacturer name

or part number if they are
printed circuit test points,

and we don't even need
to worry about them,

but they still appear
in the Parameter Manager
for you to check.
Let's take a look at another example
of really good parameterization,
this time from Daniel Gregorious.

Now, we just recently filmed
this one-minute design review,

and this parameterization
is also very good.
Now, if I open up the Parameter Manager
and just scroll over here to the right,
you'll see here

that when we get to the
manufacturer part number column,

we have pretty much every
single entry filled in.

The only thing that's really
missing from this design

is all of the entries for
the manufacturer name.

However, all of these components
can still be purchased

because we have the
manufacturer part number.

All you would have to do is
export your bill of materials,

you could upload it to
Octopart in the free BOM tool.
You could also upload it
to a distributor website like DigiKey,
and they're going to be able

to instantly identify
all of the manufacturers
for those part numbers.
Now, this type of parameterization
from (indistinct) and Daniel Gregorious

is exactly what we want
to have in our design

if we are exporting a bill
of materials to an Excel file
and we want to make sure
that all of the required information

appears in that bill of
materials automatically.
Now, let's go back to that original design
or that first design we were looking at
when we started this video.

Now, what do we do when
we have a situation

where we have some
different parameter names
inside the Parameter Manager

and we want to make sure
that they're all consistent?

Well, there's a very
simple way to handle this
inside the Parameter Manager
because the Parameter Manager

allows you to rename
some of these columns,

and that's going to rename
the corresponding parameter
inside those parts
without you having to navigate to the part
and change it manually.
So, what we're going to do
is we're gonna take these 1N4148 diodes

and we're gonna change
the part number parameter
so that it matches the parameter naming
for these Vishay diodes over here
in this part of the Parameter Manager.
Now, you can see here from the column name

that these Vishay diodes
all have the parameter name
Manufacturer Part Number.
So, what we can do

is we can go back over
here to these two diodes,
we can then right-click here,
and then we can click Rename Column.
Now, this is where we're going to enter in
the new name for this parameter.

I'm going to type in
Manufacturer Part Number
and then hit Enter.

Now, you'll see here it
doesn't change immediately.
What happens is there's a button down here
that says Accept Changes, Create ECO.
Once we click the accept change button,

we're going to then see an
Engineering Change Order pop up,
and if we hit Execute Changes,
we'll see the green check boxes.

That means it completed
successfully without errors.

Now, when I navigate
over to those two diodes,
D1 and D2,
you'll see here that if I zoom in
and select that part

and then click Show More
in the parameter list,

you'll see here that the
Manufacturer Part Number
appears right there.

So, originally it was
just named PartNumber.
Now, it's been renamed automatically
to Manufacturer Part Number,
and I didn't have to go through

and manually navigate to
all of these different parts

and look through the parameters
or do any of that stuff,

the Parameter Manager handles
it for me automatically.
Now, ideally,

you should try to enforce
consistent parameterization

in your design process and
in your design libraries,
but it's understandable

that parts sometimes
fall through the cracks.
That's why using the Parameter Manager

is a really great final
step to clean up the design
before you lock your schematics
and before you finalize the PCB layout.
Once that parameterization is cleaned up,
you'll be able to quickly
and easily export a bill of materials
into an Excel file that is complete

and won't create any
questions from your assembler.
Thanks for watching this video, everybody.
I hope this informs your design process
and helps you quickly and accurately

export a complete build of
materials for your designs.

Make sure to leave your
comments and questions
in the comments section,

and if you leave a great
question about Altium

or any other PCB design topic
in the comments section,

it just might end up
in one of these videos.
And last but not least,
make sure to call your fabricator, folks.
We'll see you next time.
